To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a single mutation that destabilizes the closed conformation allows small molecules to enter the active sites of the E. coli thymidilate synthase (EcTs) dimer and that the binding of a cofactor in one active site triggers hydide transfer and borrows stabilization from binding of substrate in the other site.
the C-terminal carboyxyl group of EcTS plays a critical role in the hydride transfer reaction.

the asymmetric structure of the C-terminally truncated EcTS in complex with substrate and CB3717 provides a structural basis for the half-sites reactivities of the mutant and explains the asymmetric distribution of β-ME adduction at different cofactor concentrations.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the structure shows how the closed state is stabilized by substrate and cofactor binding at both active sites.
a single mutation traps a half-site reactive enzyme in midstream, explaining asymmetry in hydride transfer.

the structure of the enzyme-substrate-cofactor complex shows how the binding at the active site of the cofactor and the substrate are coupled, so that the binding of one stabilizes the other, leading to hydride transfer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a single mutation that destabilizes the closed conformation can trap the enzyme in midstream and explain asymmetric reactivity.
a single mutation in a half-sites reactive enzyme can cause the enzyme to trap in an intermediate state that shows the asymmetry in the enzyme that is required for half-sites reactivities.

we have solved the structure of the C terminal deletion mutant of Ec TS in complex with CB3717 and a substrate, and that the structure shows how the boronate inhibitor binds to only one active site and that this is consistent with the observed asymmetric reactivity of the enzyme.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the asymmetric structure of the C-terminally truncated EcTS complex is consistent with the asymmetric reactivity observed for this protein, and the asymmetry of the structure can be understood in terms of the half-sites reactivities observed for this protein.
the structure of the mutant enzyme is not a simple reflection of the equilibrium mixture of products and reactants, but rather reflects a snapshot in the transition state of hydride transfer.
the C-terminal carboyxyl group of EcTS is essential to the catalytic mechanism, not only for sealing the active site but also for triggering hydride transfer.
